title: The Devil Wears Prada
wpTitle: The Devil Wears Prada Reviews – A reviews round-up for the new musical at the West End's Dominion Theatre

ratings.excerpt: Absolutely fabulous … The beloved film’s West End makeover is fun, full of knowing humour – and packed with Elton John’s irresistible songs … Elton John’s irresistible songs are the highlight of this big, bold, metaphorically shoulder-padded musical, which also features a star turn from Vanessa Williams as Miranda Priestly, wintry supremo of Manhattan fashion magazine Runway. … The tunes, from disco to power pop to Broadway homage, are draped in witty lyrics by Shaina Taub and Mark Sonnenblick, and belted out by a glamazon cast in a ritzy, glitzy production by director and choreographer Jerry Mitchell that conquers the cavernous Dominion. … For the OTT ball scene costumier Gregg Barnes creates a series of ravishing, demonic creations that distract from the fact that the accompanying title

Show’s a knock-off but it’s Devil of a good time … ... Broadway star Vanessa Williams steps into Meryl’s shoes as Miranda. She rises through the stages as if on an elevator from hell, to roars of approval. Having played a fashion editor in TV’s Ugly Betty, she was a shoo-in for the role and handles dialogue like a spitting cobra. … Outstanding contributions come from Matt Henry as Miranda’s gay stylist Nigel – his song Seen is a heartbreaking highlight … Hats off to the designers, who add the frizzle to the couture catwalk, and the dazzling sets revolve with choreographic regularity, lashing us into cartoon chapters. … There are inevitable factors that work against the plot: the arc is a bit predictable, and the vulnerability beneath Miranda’s armoured carapace feels forced. However, it is

More John Lewis than Valentino … Audiences at the Dominion Theatre in London will find that this retread of the 2006 movie, with songs by Elton John, is efficient, well-groomed and, at times, a tiny bit dull … Aside from the few occasions where Elton John’s music catches fire and the designers begin to throw colour around (there’s a suave red-white-and-blue motif when the story shifts to Paris), the director-choreographer Jerry Mitchell’s retread of the 2006 Hollywood film is efficient, well-groomed and, at times, a tiny bit dull. … As anyone who saw her in Ugly Betty knows, Vanessa Williams — who plays Miranda here — can turn on the hauteur. She’s an accomplished singer too, yet you’re still left with the impression that you’re looking at a photocopy of a Technicolor original. … Georgie B

I wanted to love or loathe The Devil Wears Prada but… … Elton John’s Voguetastic new musical is enjoyable — but where’s the magic? … It is based on a quite good film (I know, I know, others love it). Crucially, it’s got plenty of quite good songs, and maybe two or three very good songs. It retraces the steps of the film quite well, and every now and then — usually in tandem with the very good songs — sprouts into something very theatrical and wonderful. It’s acted, sung, danced and designed very well. It’s enjoyable without quite being magical. … It’s all decently done. The director and choreographer Jerry Mitchell knows his way round a set piece. I only wish there were more of them. … So I don’t mean to be sour: The Devil Wears Prada is solidly entertaining.

The Devil Wears Prada musical is about as groundbreaking as florals for spring … Come for the fabulous frocks, not for Elton John’s forgettable songs or the naff dance routines … ... does this theatrical version complete a gilded hat-trick of triumphs? To some extent, comes my qualified answer as an admirer of both Lauren Weisberger’s book and Aline Brosh McKenna’s whip-smart screenplay, so memorably brought to life by Anne Hathaway, Emily Blunt and Meryl Streep. It’s such a strong and appealing story that it’s a delight to see these characters pop up in another medium, although how it fares as a standalone piece of new musical theatre is a far less certain matter. … The costumes are, of course, fabulous, and Williams, a made-to-measure fit for the Priestly part as the undisputed mistress

Prosecco o’clock musical is old hat … It is dressed to impress and has powerhouse singing from Vanessa Williams but this retread of the hit book and film rings hollow … o big or go home … A prosecco o’clock musical, briskly directed and choreographed by Jerry Mitchell, that replicates the 2006 film starring Meryl Streep and Anne Hathaway to within an inch of its haute couture-clad life, but without capturing its icy heart. … To give the show its due, the production values are high, Shaina Taub and Mark Sonnenblick’s lyrics are serviceable and John’s music exuberant. Vanessa Williams is a powerhouse singer as editor-in-chief Miranda Priestly, with songs like the clubby House of Miranda, and so is Georgie Buckland as her young, ambitious assistant, Andy. Visually it is nothing if not impress

Even Elton John can’t save this truly diabolical adaptation of The Devil Wears Prada … ‘Desperate Housewives’ star Vanessa Williams turns in a decent performance as the fearsome Miranda Priestly, but this West End production feels frozen in time … You’d hope that enlisting Elton John to write the songs would guarantee any musical entry into the former category but, alas, The Devil Wears Prada is truly diabolical. … It’s not the fault of star Vanessa Williams, who turns in a decent performance as fictional magazine editor Miranda Priestly – acting with a subtlety that her fearsome red-and-black costumes lack. Instead, it’s a result of a lack of imagination from the whole writing team, who cling to the 2006 film’s script like a millennial clings to stretch denim jeans (they’re more comfy, OK

Spangly and shallow … Lavish stage adaptation of the hit film looks good, but has nothing to say … What’s the opposite of devil’s advocate? Because there’s little to advocate for in this brute-force funnelling of a good film so blandly on to the stage. … As a comment on the fashion industry, it sort of nails it. It looks impressive, in a spangly, shallow way, and convinces itself it has something to say in order to disguise its preening vacuity. As a musical it’s pretty and uninteresting, shot through with the kind of obviousness and mediocrity that Miranda Priestly would abhor. … The two best things about the production are Georgie Buckland playing Andy and Amy di Bartolomeo as Emily. It’s quite a West End debut from Buckland, dominating even when up against the star power of Vanessa Will

Elton John’s so-so musical is no match for Meryl Streep … Generic songs, a derivative script and a daunting act to follow add up to a film-to-stage adaptation that’s shiny but skimpy … The old saying goes that the devil has all the best tunes. But that isn’t borne out by this shiny yet bafflingly skimpy musical version of The Devil Wears Prada … Style as well as (some) substance is required here, and you’d think that’d be here in abundance given that Elton John has written the music. But it’s as if the trendsetter who gave us Billy Elliot and The Lion King – not to mention some of the finest pop songs of our era – has couriered over some generic material and everyone has followed suit (the bland lyrics are by Shaina Taub and Mark Sonnenblick). … Jerry Mitchell’s fleet but rote production h

A slim, superficial musical … Not even Elton John’s songs can redeem this predictable show at London’s Dominion Theatre … There’s an ice queen, a ball and a transformation scene, but no, we’re not at a pantomime. This is the world of high fashion as depicted in the spindly heeled musical version of The Devil Wears Prada. And forget good versus evil — here the stakes are really high. … Jerry Mitchell’s glossy staging leans into the associations suggested by the show’s title … Fans of the movie may enjoy revelling in key droll moments, choice bitchy lines, and the sheer poise of Williams’ Miranda, and this was never going to be a musical in the Sondheim vein.
